paragraphs: Swamiji once knew a very old yogi, Pavhari Baba of Ghazipur, who lived alone in a hole dug in the ground. He owned almost nothing: a pan or two to cook in, hardly any clothes, and very little food. Most of his hours went into meditation.

What made him remarkable was how he saw others. He had reached a state where he would harm no one, because in every person and every animal he saw the same Soul, the Lord of the universe. He never called anyone by any other name. Everyone, human or animal, was "my Lord" to him.

One day a thief crept in and made off with one of his pans. The old man saw him and ran after him. It was a long chase, and finally the thief had to stop, worn out. The yogi caught up, dropped to his knees in front of him, and thanked him for the honour of his visit. Then he held out the second pan and begged him to take that as well, since it too belonged to him.

Swamiji said that Pavhari Baba loved everything in the world so deeply that he would have given his life for an ant. Even wild creatures sensed that he was their friend. Snakes and fierce animals would come into his hollow and sleep beside him, and in his presence they never fought.
learn: Most of us chase after people to get back what they took. This story turns that instinct upside down. You may not hand your phone to a thief, but you can practise seeing the person behind the behaviour, and that changes how you respond to people who wrong you.
